```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE, error = FALSE)
```

One YAML file describes a whole run, and `platypus_spec()` reads it. This is the walk
through that file; the exhaustive list of fields lives on the engine's site, because the
file is the engine's format and keeping a second copy here would mean two of them going
out of step:
[every configuration field](https://maju116.github.io/pyplatypus/config.html).

**The same file works in both packages.** R reads it with `platypus_spec()`, Python with
`from_yaml()`, and both hand it to the same validator. Nothing below is R-specific except
the lines that run it.

Arguments and YAML produce the same object and nothing downstream can tell which was used,
so a configuration file and an R script describe the same experiment - and either can be
handed to a colleague.

## One file, one run

The shortest thing that trains:

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: first_try
    input_shape: [256, 256]
```

```{r}
spec <- platypus_spec("run.yaml")
fit <- platypus_fit(spec)
evaluate(fit)
```

Four things are required and the rest have defaults: `task`, `data.train_path`, and a
`name` and `input_shape` for each model. Everything else - the architecture, the loss, the
optimiser, how many epochs - has a default that lives in the engine, so **a short
configuration is a complete one** rather than an incomplete one. `?u_net` has a *Where the
defaults live* section saying why they are not written into the R signatures.

`colormap` says which colour in a mask means which class, darkest first. Masks stored as
label maps rather than pictures use `labels: [0, 1]` instead, and giving both is an error:
exactly one says how a mask is encoded.

## Several models at once

`models:` is a list, and that is the reason this file format exists rather than only the
code path. Each entry trains on the same data and lands in the same table, so comparing
variants is one run rather than a loop somebody has to write.

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: shallow
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    blocks: 3
    filters: 16
  - name: deep
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    blocks: 5
    filters: 32
    architecture: u_net_plus_plus
```

```{r}
fit <- platypus_fit(platypus_spec("run.yaml"))
evaluate(fit)            # one row per model
training_history(fit)    # one row per model per epoch
```

`name` has to be unique, because it is how a model is identified in every score table, in
every record and in `predict(fit, model = ...)`. Two models called the same thing is
refused rather than resolved, by name:
`model names must be unique; repeated: shallow`.

Two entries differing only in `blocks` is a legitimate configuration and a common one: this
is for comparing variants, not only architectures.

## Dividing one folder

With no `validation_path`, say how to divide `train_path`:

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/all
  split:
    fractions: [0.7, 0.15, 0.15]
    group_by: "^(patient\\d+)_"
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: by_patient
    input_shape: [256, 256]
```

Two fractions give train and validation, three add a test set. Nothing is written to disk -
the samples are divided after they are discovered, so there are no new folders and no CSV.
`split_dataset()` is still the tool when the CSVs themselves are the point.

**`group_by` is required and may be `NULL`.** It is a regular expression whose first group
is the thing that must not appear on both sides - a patient, a scan, a slide. The mistake it
prevents leaves no trace: slices of one patient in both sets make validation measure memory
rather than generalisation, and every number in the output still looks reasonable. An
omitted key would be that choice made silently; `null` is the same choice made on purpose,
for data where every sample is independent.

Exactly one of `split` and `validation_path`. If a run genuinely has no validation set - a
final fit on everything - say `validation: false`, which is the third answer rather than an
absence, because "I have no validation set" and "I forgot" look identical otherwise.

The same from R, where the argument answers the same question three ways:

```{r}
segmentation_data("data/all", split = list(fractions = c(0.8, 0.2), group_by = NULL))
segmentation_data("data/train", validation = "data/validation")
segmentation_data("data/all", validation = FALSE)
```

## Augmentation, callbacks, and the rest of a model

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: augmented
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    epochs: 40
    loss: {name: dice}
    metrics: [{name: iou}, {name: dice}]
    optimizer: {name: adam, learning_rate: 0.001}
    callbacks:
      - {name: early_stopping, monitor: val_loss, patience: 10}
      - {name: model_checkpoint, monitor: val_iou, path: runs/best.safetensors}
    augmentation:
      - {name: HorizontalFlip, params: {p: 0.5}}
      - {name: RandomBrightnessContrast, params: {p: 0.3}}
```

Every one of those blocks has an R constructor that builds the same thing, and the help
pages for them are where the measurements are: `?losses`, `?metrics`, `?optimizers`,
`?callbacks`.

```{r}
u_net(
  "augmented",
  input_shape = c(256, 256),
  epochs = 40,
  loss = loss_dice(),
  metrics = list(metric_iou(), metric_dice()),
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.001),
  callbacks = list(
    callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_loss", patience = 10),
    callback_model_checkpoint(monitor = "val_iou", path = "runs/best.safetensors")
  ),
  augmentation = list(
    augmentation_step("HorizontalFlip", p = 0.5),
    augmentation_step("RandomBrightnessContrast", p = 0.3)
  )
)
```

**There is no `mode` on a callback that watches a number.** The direction is taken from the
name: anything ending in `loss` is better lower, anything else better higher. So
`monitor = "val_iou"` maximises and `monitor = "val_loss"` minimises, and there is nothing
to set inconsistently.

**Augmentation applies to the training data only** - never to validation, where the point is
to measure the same thing every epoch. The names are albumentations' own, and
`available_transforms()` lists what the installed version offers; at `rank = 3` the list is
shorter, because support for volumes is uneven. Each step is probed at the model's own input
size while the pipeline is built, so a transform that cannot do the job says so before the
first epoch rather than during it.

## Overlapping classes instead of one per voxel

`colormap` and `labels` both say the same thing about a voxel: it is in exactly one class.
`regions` is the third way of naming classes and the only one that drops that assumption -
classes named as unions of a label map's values, which is how BraTS and the
lesion-inside-an-organ family actually store their ground truth.

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  regions:
    - {name: whole tumour, of: [1, 2, 4]}
    - {name: tumour core, of: [1, 4]}
    - {name: enhancing, of: [4]}
models:
  - name: brats
    input_shape: [240, 240]
    loss: {name: focal}
```

The same from R. A region is a `list(name = , of = )`, and `of` takes the label-map values
that belong to it:

```{r}
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    "data/train", "data/validation",
    regions = list(
      list(name = "whole tumour", of = c(1, 2, 4)),
      list(name = "tumour core", of = c(1, 4)),
      list(name = "enhancing", of = 4)
    )
  ),
  models = list(u_net("brats", input_shape = c(240, 240), loss = loss_focal()))
)
```

The last region shows that a single value is **ordinary** rather than an edge case: BraTS's
enhancing tumour is one label.

The task is still `semantic_segmentation`. What changes is what a channel means.

**There is no background entry, so the class count is not the one you would write as
`labels`.** Those same masks as `labels = c(0, 1, 2, 4)` are **four** classes; as the three
regions above they are **three** channels. And a voxel whose value is `4` is in all three of
them at once, which is the point rather than a tolerated side effect.

**Each channel is an independent binary question** - a sigmoid per channel rather than one
softmax across them - so the channels do not compete and do not sum to one. That is what
makes the overlap expressible, and it is also why a prediction cannot be written back as a
single picture with `save_masks()`: one voxel gets one colour, and a voxel here may belong to
three classes.

So `save_masks()` refuses such a prediction rather than taking the strongest channel, and
`predict()` refuses `type = "class"` for the same reason - there is no one class per voxel to
return. Ask for `type = "probability"` and write it with `save_class_masks()`, which gives one
binary file per region, named after the region. The channel order is the order the regions
were written in, which is also the order `inspect_masks()` names them in and the order every
per-class score is reported in.

**Two regions are the minimum**, because one region is ordinary binary segmentation and
`labels = c(0, 1)` already says that - with a background channel, which `regions` has none
of. Disjoint regions are allowed and are not a mistake: they group several values into one
class and drop the background channel, which is a useful thing to ask for and is refused
nowhere.

**The failure this invites is quiet, so it is refused loudly.** A region whose `of` matches
nothing in the data - `of = 3` against a label map holding `1`, `2` and `4` - is a channel of
zeros. It trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 for that region while every other
number in the run looks ordinary, which is the kind of result that gets read as "that class
is hard". `platypus_fit()` refuses it before training, and `inspect_masks()` asks the same
question over as much of the data as you want - **naming the region rather than giving its
position**, because `missing_classes: 1` would leave you counting entries in the file above:

```{r}
inspect_masks(spec)
#>   split unmatched samples_checked total_samples present_classes      missing_classes
#> 1 train    0.0000             500          1251 whole tumour, ...    enhancing
```

### When the overlap was drawn separately: `classes_from`

`regions` needs the overlap to be a union of one label map's values, which is how BraTS
stores it: one integer per voxel, and the scored classes are conventions over those
integers. Some overlaps are not like that. A vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators'
masks of the same structure, were drawn independently, and no single integer can hold both.
Those arrive as **one binary file per class**, and `classes_from` names them - one pattern
per class, in class order, matched against a sample's mask files.

```{r}
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    "data/train", "data/validation",
    classes_from = c("_vessel\\.png$", "_organ\\.png$")
  ),
  models = list(u_net("crossing", input_shape = c(256, 256)))
)
```

Everything above still holds: independent binary questions, no background entry, a
prediction `save_masks()` refuses and `save_class_masks()` writes. The difference between
the two namings is the file on disk and nothing else.

**Every pattern must match exactly one of a sample's mask files, and every mask file must
match a pattern.** Both halves are refused, because each is invisible from the other side: a
pattern matching nothing is a class the model is never shown, and a file matching no pattern
is a class the data has and nobody asked for. Patterns are Python regular expressions, like
`channels_from` and `group_by`, so R's own backslashes double.

The order is written rather than inferred, and here it matters more than for channels: a
model trained with the vessel in the first channel and used where the first channel is the
organ answers plausibly, in range, and nothing further down can notice.

## Instances instead of one mask

`task: instance_segmentation` keeps the objects apart rather than uniting them. The data
block gets **shorter** rather than longer: no `colormap` and no `labels`, because there are
always exactly two classes - background and object - and what names the objects is the
directory of per-object mask files itself.

```yaml
task: instance_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  mode: nested_dirs
models:
  - name: rim
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    separation: {name: rim, width: 2}
    loss: {name: cce_dice}
    decode: [{name: nearest_seed}, {name: connected_components}]
  - name: flows
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    separation:
      name: flows
      loss: {name: mse, where: foreground}
```

The same two models from R. `instance_data()` is what says which task this is - an instance
data block declares nothing a segmentation one lacks, so the constructor is the word:

```{r}
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = instance_data("data/train", "data/validation"),
  models = list(
    u_net(
      "rim",
      input_shape = c(256, 256),
      separation = separation_rim(width = 2),
      loss = loss_cce_dice(),
      decode = list(decode_nearest_seed(), decode_connected_components())
    ),
    u_net(
      "flows",
      input_shape = c(256, 256),
      separation = separation_flows(loss = loss_mse(where = "foreground"))
    )
  )
)
fit <- platypus_fit(spec)
evaluate(fit)
```

Two axes, and they are deliberately different shapes. **`separation` is one block per model
and has no default**: it is what the network is trained to predict, so it sets the width of
the head - three channels for `rim`, four for `flows` at two classes - and that width is
derived rather than written anywhere. **`decode` is a list**, because several decodings share
one forward pass: a second decoding of 134 images costs 1.41 s against an hour and a half for
a second training run. `evaluate()` then returns a row per *model and decoding*.

**Which mask column to read is a decision the table makes for you and it used to make it
wrongly.** Every row carries `foreground_dice` - the binary overlap of anything the model
called an object against anything that is one, the same arithmetic whatever the separation
is - and that is the one to read *across* models. The `dice` beside it is the training
metric, a mean over the class channels the head has, so three for `separation_rim()` against
two for `separation_flows()`: read down one model's rows, never across two. On the Data
Science Bowl's validation cases the class column showed two masks 0.09 apart that are 0.0062
apart, and in the other direction.

**No value appears in both lists**, which is what settles which field a new idea belongs in:
`separation` is a noun and `decode` is a verb. `separation_rim()` can be decoded by
`decode_nearest_seed()` or `decode_watershed()`, `separation_flows()` by
`decode_follow_flows()`, and `decode_connected_components()` reads no signal at all and works
with every target. Leave `decode` out and it derives to the signal's own decoding plus
`connected_components`; give a list and you get the list you gave.

A model's own `loss` and `metrics` score the mask at either separation, so they are an
overlap or a cross-entropy loss here as everywhere else. `separation_flows()` carries its own
`loss` for the two vector channels, which is where `loss_mse()`, `loss_l1()` and
`loss_smooth_l1()` belong: `where = "foreground"` averages the error over the voxels the
target is defined on, and on these images that is 13.97% of them.

**What this task is worth is measured, and it is not flattering.** On the Data Science Bowl
the separation signal is worth +0.068 of instance average precision at best while a perfect
mask is worth +0.2398, so the mask is the limit by a factor of 3.6 - and a *perfect* semantic
mask decoded by `connected_components` still scores only 0.7655. That is what the yardstick
row is for: a run that improved the mask and did nothing for the separation improves every
row at once, and without the row that ignores the signal there is nothing to notice it
against.

**One thing is missing from R rather than from the engine, and it is missing on purpose
rather than by oversight**: `predict()` on an instance fit refuses. The run and its scores
work - `evaluate()` gives the row per model and decoding above - but there is no call yet
that brings the objects themselves back into R as a label map, so `predict()` says so
instead of returning a mask that is not what you asked for. `platypus#103`.

## Detection instead of segmentation

`task: object_detection` changes which fields the file accepts. Boxes rather than masks, so
`classes` and an annotation format rather than a colormap:

```yaml
task: object_detection
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  annotation_format: pascal_voc
  classes: [rbc, wbc, platelets]
models:
  - name: cells
    input_shape: [416, 416]
```

**Leave `anchors` out and they are fitted to your own boxes** by k-means on an IoU distance,
`anchors_per_grid` of them per grid. That is worth about 0.23 of mean overlap against COCO's
nine on blood cells - measured, 0.65 against 0.88 - so the default is the useful one and
naming anchors by hand is for reproducing a published model. `detection_anchors()` reports
them and `plot_anchors()` draws them against the boxes they were fitted to.

## One label instead of a mask

`task: classification` answers with one label for a whole image rather than one per voxel.
The data block loses everything that describes a mask and gains the one thing a label
needs - `classes`, in class order:

```yaml
task: classification
data:
  train_path: data/train
  validation_path: data/validation
  mode: nested_dirs
  classes: [benign, malignant]
models:
  - name: ours
    input_shape: [128, 128]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    loss: {name: cce}
    metrics: [{name: auc}, {name: balanced_accuracy}]
  - name: resnet
    input_shape: [224, 224]
    encoder: resnet34
    pretrained: true
    freeze_encoder: 2
    pooling: max
    head_dropout: 0.2
    loss: {name: focal, gamma: 2}
```

The same thing from code is `classification_data()` and `classifier()`:

```{r}
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = classification_data("data/train", "data/validation",
                             classes = c("benign", "malignant")),
  models = list(
    classifier("ours", input_shape = c(128, 128), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
               loss = loss_cce(),
               metrics = list(metric_auc(), metric_balanced_accuracy())),
    classifier("resnet", input_shape = c(224, 224), encoder = "resnet34",
               pretrained = TRUE, freeze_encoder = 2, pooling = "max",
               head_dropout = 0.2, loss = loss_focal(gamma = 2))
  )
)
```

**Where the labelling is written follows from `mode` rather than being said twice.** In
`nested_dirs` the directories under `train_path` are the classes, with the images inside
them - the layout nearly every image dataset ships in - and in `config_file` the CSV's
`label` column holds the name. `subdirs` is refused here, which is what keeps the two
readings of `nested_dirs` apart: a sample is one image rather than a directory with the
image in one subdirectory and what labels it in the other.

**`classifier()` is the one model constructor in this package not named after an
architecture**, and the missing field is the point rather than an omission. The network is a
contracting path, pooled, with one dense layer on top, so `encoder` is the whole answer:
unset it is ours, sized by `blocks` and `filters`, and named it is any of
`available_encoders()`. The two models above are the comparison this task makes easiest -
ours against a pretrained backbone on the same split. `blocks`, `filters` and `block_width`
are **refused** beside `encoder` rather than ignored, because a backbone's own depth is then
the only one there is, and `available_models("classification")` says all of this instead of
returning rows.

**`metric_auc()` is the default and that is a measurement rather than a preference.** On
40000 images at a prevalence of 3%, with the model's own probabilities as the truth so that
only its discrimination varies, accuracy spans 0.0100 where the AUC spans 0.4631 - and
accuracy is not monotone in quality: the model with no signal at all scores above two that
have one. `metric_balanced_accuracy()` and `metric_f1()` do not rescue it, moving 0.0000 and
-0.0005 between a real signal and a collapse, because a calibrated model at that prevalence
never crosses the threshold and everything read off the hard prediction sees the same
all-negative answer. `class_balance()` is what makes that prevalence visible before a run
rather than after it.

**A split cut out of the training folder is stratified**, which is the one part of the walk
this task overrides. Measured over 400 seeds, a random 70/15/15 of 100 images at a 3%
prevalence leaves some part with none of the rare class 91% of the time, 64% at 200 images
and 20% at 500 - and a per-class metric cannot average over a class its pass never held, so
the run dies at the end of the first epoch with the epoch already paid for. `group_by`
beside it is refused when a group's images do not share a label, because keeping a patient
on one side and keeping a class on both are then two instructions that cannot both be
followed.

**What `predict()` gives back is a table rather than an array**, which is the shape the rest
of R wants. `type = "class"` is one row per image with `key`, `label`, `predicted` and
`probability`, and `type = "probability"` is a matrix of images by classes with the keys as
row names - so either one joins to whatever else you hold per image. `space` and the
`cases`/`each` pair are refused by name: they describe a grid, and a split of masks too
large to hold at once, and neither is a thing one label per image has.
`evaluate_cases()` is refused for a different reason - a case here is one image whose score
is 0 or 1, so a split's worst case is 0 for any model that gets a single image wrong.

### When the label is a set: `labels_from`

A chest film with four findings is **four independent questions** rather than one of four
alternatives, and `labels_from` is how that is said: one CSV column per class, in class
order, each cell `0` or `1`.

```yaml
task: classification
data:
  train_path: data/train.csv
  validation_path: data/validation.csv
  mode: config_file
  classes: [atelectasis, effusion, nodule, mass]
  labels_from: [Atelectasis, Effusion, Nodule, Mass]
models:
  - name: ours
    input_shape: [224, 224]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
    loss: {name: cce}
    metrics: [{name: auc}, {name: f1}]
```

The same thing from code:

```{r}
spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = classification_data(
    "data/train.csv", "data/validation.csv",
    classes = c("atelectasis", "effusion", "nodule", "mass"),
    labels_from = c("Atelectasis", "Effusion", "Nodule", "Mass"),
    mode = "config_file"
  ),
  models = list(
    classifier("ours", input_shape = c(224, 224), blocks = 4, filters = 16,
               loss = loss_cce(), metrics = list(metric_auc(), metric_f1()))
  )
)
```

**It is a naming rather than a switch**, for the reason `regions` and `classes_from` are on
the mask side: the *target* changes and not only the activation. A `label` column
structurally cannot say a film has two findings, so a `multilabel = TRUE` would have trained
sigmoid channels against an exclusive target, raised nothing, and reported plausible numbers
meaning exactly what softmax meant.

**Position is the pairing.** The headers may be called whatever the dataset calls them -
above they are capitalised and the classes are not - and the model still learns the classes
in the order `classes` names them. `config_file` only, because an image cannot sit in two
directories without being two files, and `strict_labels` is refused beside it rather than
ignored: the columns *are* the classes, so no cell can hold a class nobody named.

A cell that is not `0`, `1`, `0.0` or `1.0` is refused by name, and the case it is written
for is `-1`. The datasets shaped this way write `-1` for *uncertain* and leave the cell empty
for *not mentioned*; both have a defensible mapping, which is exactly why the reader must not
pick one for you. An image with none of the findings is an ordinary labelled row, written as
a line of zeros.

**`metric_accuracy()` is refused here rather than redefined.** On 4000 images with findings
at 10%, 5%, 3% and 2%, a model answering no to everything scores **0.8137** on exact match
and **0.9507** per class - above a model holding half the available signal - so neither
reading of it can be what a `monitor` watches. Use `metric_balanced_accuracy()`,
`metric_f1()` or `metric_auc()`.

**`predict()` answers in a different shape on this route**, because the answer is a different
kind of thing: one row per image *per class*, with `key`, `class`, and `label` and
`predicted` as logicals. An image with none of the findings is a row of `FALSE` per class
rather than an empty cell, which could also mean unread - and a split **nobody labelled** is
`NA`, which is the other half of that sentence and the reason `FALSE` can be trusted to mean
*measured and absent*. There is no `probability` column - that column is the chosen class's
own number, and with independent questions nothing was chosen - so `type = "probability"` is
the whole of the answer there, one column per class.

### Predicting on images you have no labels for

A test set is often just pictures, and that is an ordinary thing to have rather than a
half-written configuration. Name them in a CSV with no label column - `key, images` and
nothing else - and the split is read as unlabelled:

```yaml
task: classification
data:
  train_path: data/train.csv
  validation_path: data/validation.csv
  test_path: data/to-predict.csv
  mode: config_file
  classes: [benign, malignant]
models:
  - name: ours
    input_shape: [224, 224]
    blocks: 4
    filters: 16
```

`predict()` and `evaluate()` then differ in what they can honestly do with it:

- **`predict()` works**, and that is what the split is for. `label` comes back as `NA`
  rather than as a class name or as `FALSE` per class, because nothing said.
- **`evaluate()` refuses it by name.** Scoring against labels that are not there would
  either fail somewhere inside the metric or, worse, report a number - and a zero in a
  table is read as a result.
- **`class_balance()` refuses it too**, for the same reason: counted anyway it says every
  class has no images, which reads as a finding about the dataset rather than about there
  being nothing to count.

The `key` column is what makes the answer joinable to whatever else you hold - a pixel size,
a patient identifier, a date - so it is worth writing even where the row order would do.

**One layout cannot do this and the refusal says so.** `nested_dirs` makes the directory the
label, so there is no unlabelled form of it: an image has to sit somewhere, and where it sits
is the answer. Point `test_path` at a CSV instead, or at the images themselves.

## Not training at all

```yaml
task: semantic_segmentation
data:
  train_path: data/images
  validation_path: data/images
  colormap: [[0, 0, 0], [255, 255, 255]]
models:
  - name: published
    input_shape: [256, 256]
    weights: dsbowl-unet
    fit: false
```

`weights` takes a registry name, a local path, or `hf://owner/repo/file@commit` - and the
`hf://` form requires the commit, because weights that change under a stable name are the
worst kind of irreproducibility. A registry name carries one already;
`available_weights()` lists them.

With `fit: false` nothing trains and `predict(fit)` works immediately. The weights are
checked against the model they are being loaded into *before* torch is touched: a shape, a
channel count or a class count that does not match is a refusal naming the field, not a
tensor-size error from inside a loss.

## What is checked, and when

Validation happens in this order, and the first two cost no epochs:

1. **The file, against the schema.** Unknown fields, missing required ones, a `name:` that no
   block has, a callback watching a number nothing will produce. Before any path is read -
   and before Python starts, for the checks R can make itself.
2. **The data on disk**, when the run begins: that the folders exist, that images and masks
   correspond, and that every class in `colormap` or `labels` actually appears in the masks,
   because a declared class appearing in none has a target channel of zeros, so the model is
   never shown what it is being asked to find. `inspect_masks()` runs that check on its own,
   and `platypus_fit(check_masks = FALSE)` skips it.
3. **Everything else**, during the run.

A refusal names the field and says what to do. The engine's own messages are translated into
R conditions rather than passed through as Python tracebacks, so
`tryCatch(platypus_spec("run.yaml"), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))` gives a
sentence rather than a stack.

## The same run from code

The file is not a second implementation. These describe the same experiment:

```{r}
spec <- platypus_spec("run.yaml")

spec <- platypus_spec(
  data = segmentation_data(
    "data/train",
    validation = "data/validation",
    colormap = list(c(0, 0, 0), c(255, 255, 255))
  ),
  models = list(u_net("first_try", input_shape = c(256, 256)))
)
```

And `as.list(spec)` is the file, so a run built from arguments can be written out and kept:

```{r}
yaml::write_yaml(as.list(spec), "run.yaml")
```

Which to use is a question about how many models and how often, not about what is possible.
A file is better when there are several models, when the run is going to be repeated, or
when somebody else has to see what was done; the arguments are better inside a loop over
something the file cannot express, like a vector of datasets.

Note that `as.list()` is also how the fields are reached: the object returned by
`platypus_spec()` carries the specification on the Python side, so `spec$task` is `NULL`
while `as.list(spec)$task` is what you want.
